Oxygen supply for your fish in exceptional situations
How to Care for Your Aquarium Fish During a Power Outage
How to Use Airline Accessories with an Aquarium Air Pump
Aquarium Aeration: What It Is & Why It's Important
Máy sủi oxy cho bể cá: Cách sử dụng đúng và bảo dưỡng bền lâu

facts.fact: Fish and the biofilter bacteria both use dissolved oxygen, so aeration and water circulation are essential.
Dissolved oxygen should be kept above 5.0 mg/L throughout the system.
Above 5 mg/L dissolved oxygen is best for most finfish, and fish become stressed below 5 mg/L.
Low dissolved oxygen and high ammonia are the two water problems most likely to kill fish directly.
Circulation lets excess carbon dioxide and nitrogen gas escape to the air.
Circulation mixes the water from top to bottom, so oxygen and temperature stay even through the tank.
A membrane (diaphragm) air pump uses an electromagnet to move a membrane up and down. Air is drawn through a felt filter and pushed out through an airstone as small bubbles.
Aeration means making a water–air contact surface where oxygen and CO2 are exchanged. A choppy, turbulent surface aerates well.
A smooth, glassy water surface gives only about 5% of the aeration of a choppy surface of the same size.
Many rising bubbles also create turbulence and aerate well, so surface agitation or bubbles can do the job.
Air-driven devices such as sponge filters, air stones and bubblers increase surface agitation and oxygen in the tank.
Finer bubbles transfer oxygen and mix the water better. Cutting bubble size from 5 mm to 2 mm can greatly improve efficiency.
An air stone is a small weighted bubbler that makes fine bubbles. This improves oxygenation and cuts bubbling noise.
Fully air-saturated water at 78°F holds about 8.25 ppm (mg/L) of oxygen.
Warm water holds less oxygen than cold water.
Air pumps help when fish need oxygen-rich water, during medication, when several water care products are used, and in summer heat, when oxygen can fall dangerously low.
Active aeration with an air pump is advised during medication or anti-algae treatment, with heavy stocking, in tanks without plants, and at night in heavily planted tanks.
Most freshwater tanks can get enough aeration from proper filtration, mainly through surface agitation.
Fish short of oxygen often gather at the surface and gulp air. This is called 'piping'.
Piping can also be caused by high nitrite or gill disease, so gasping at the surface alone does not prove low oxygen.
A fish kill from low oxygen is usually sudden, usually noticed early in the morning, and often hits large fish harder than small ones.
Low surface movement can let a film (scum) form on the water surface.
Fish oxygen use depends on fish size, feeding rate, activity and temperature. Biofilter bacteria use oxygen roughly in proportion to the ammonia reaching the filter.
In heavily planted tanks, oxygen often falls to its lowest at night or in the early morning, which can be dangerous for fish.
Oxygen need rises faster than fish length: a 2-inch fish needs about eight times the aeration of a 1-inch fish.
Some medications can reduce helpful bacteria and increase oxygen use.
During a power cut, a battery-powered air pump can keep the water aerated. If no pump is available, a water change helps.
In the first 1–2 hours of a power outage, leave the tank alone: don't feed, turn off automatic feeders, and don't change water.

In an outage lasting 8 hours or more, run an air stone or sponge filter for 1 hour, then repeat every 8 hours. Overstocked tanks, or tanks with fish gasping at the surface, may need aeration every 4 hours.
Unplug hang-on-back and canister filters during a long outage. When power returns, clean them before restarting so decayed material is not flushed into the tank.
After power returns, don't feed for 24 hours. Test ammonia and nitrite, and change water if either reads above 0 ppm.
In a hot-weather outage, move the tank to a cooler, shaded place and cool it with a battery fan. Don't float frozen bottles, because sudden temperature swings stress fish.
Fish that survive a sudden low-oxygen event are more likely to get opportunistic bacterial infections, so watch them afterwards.
Connect the pump to an air stone or sponge filter with airline tubing, then plug it in.
Fit a check valve between the pump and the device, with the flapper side facing the pump. If it is put in backwards, no air flows.
Place the check valve outside the tank near the rim, not next to the pump.
To control airflow, fit an air valve near the tank rim. Tighten it for less air and loosen it for more.
To run two devices from one outlet, use a T splitter, with an air valve on each line to balance the flow. A gang valve with its own switch on each outlet can feed several lines.
Cut airline tubing straight and cleanly, without tears.
Hanging the pump up keeps its vibration from passing into the cabinet.
Choosing size, Sera example: the sera air 110 plus suits tanks up to 100 L, the 275 R plus up to 300 L, and the 550 R plus tanks over 300 L and ponds (with weather protection).

Sera air pumps give at least 100–140 mbar, about 1.0–1.4 m of water column, so an airstone still bubbles at that depth. Joining outlets with a Y-piece raises it to about 160–170 mbar. Power draw is 3, 4 or 8 W.
Airstones aerate well only if the pump can make hundreds of bubbles per second. Small pumps sold in kits or stores do little.
A check valve stops water siphoning back out of the tank when the pump stops, for example in a power cut.
A check valve is not needed if the air pump sits higher than the tank rim.
Water leaking back can damage the pump, flood the floor and, in extreme cases, cause an electrical fire.
Check airline tubing now and then for hardening or drying, which loosens connections and can cause drips during a power cut.
Sera supplies a non-return (check) valve with each pump to stop water being drawn back into it.
Sera pumps' dust-collecting filter felt can be swapped, and the membrane block can be replaced as a spare part.
Clean diffusers periodically, since algae, food and waste clog their pores.
Very hard water (alkalinity over 400 mg/L as CaCO3) can clog solid stone diffusers with carbonate. Flexible membrane diffusers resist this better.
Aquarium Co-Op's battery air pump charges while plugged in, starts by itself when power fails, and runs about 20 hours, or about 40 hours or more in Power Save mode.
USB air pumps can run from a USB power bank or a laptop.
Heavy aeration drives CO2 down to about 2–3 ppm, while plants do best above 10 ppm, so it removes injected CO2 in planted tanks.
Vigorously aerating submerged filter beds can dislodge the beneficial bacteria.
Airstones carry moisture out of the tank and can cause significant evaporation. Choppy surface agitation is preferred in dry climates.
Even fully tightened, an air valve lets a little air escape. This stops back pressure from damaging the pump.
Each extra outlet on a gang valve weakens the output, so more outlets need more adjustment.
Check valves slightly cut the airflow a pump delivers.
Aquarium Science calls the rule of 12 square inches of surface per inch of fish common but false.
Aquarium Science says using the ratio of surface area to depth to judge aeration is meaningless.
Aquarium Science rejects the claim that diffusion alone is enough. It says moderately stocked tanks need aeration.
JBL stopped making oxygen tablets (JBL OxyTabs) because people wrongly used them in place of aeration. JBL prefers air pumps.
Vietnamese names: máy sủi oxy, máy sủi khí or máy sục khí (air pump); đá sủi or thanh sủi (air stone or bar); máy sủi tích điện, or sủi AC/DC, for battery-backup pumps.
Brands sold in Vietnam include Gex, Periha and Atman. Battery-backup pumps are suggested for power cuts and for valuable fish such as cá Rồng (arowana) and cá Koi.
Hot weather lowers dissolved oxygen, so watch the air pump more closely in the hot season.
Air stones are generally avoided in saltwater tanks because they can irritate corals and cause foam and salt creep.
